title: The Cost of Friday
focus: 说明选择、成本与必要条件
story:
The date is still Friday. It sits in the schedule in a green box, looking more certain than anything around it.

This is a possible pilot date, not the demonstration deadline we clarified earlier in the project. Nevertheless, I can feel the same temptation to let a tidy word stand for an untidy agreement. Friday in which place, for which work, under which conditions? We settle the time zone first. The more difficult questions remain.

Daniel places a budget sheet beside the schedule. “The centre has reserved staff time. If we move this, there is a cost.”

Rui folds his arms. “If we start before we're ready, there's a cost too.”

“I know. I need both costs on the table.”

His voice is flat rather than angry. I open the test report. We have corrected the repeated notification behaviour from the internal test, and the relevant checks now pass. That does not make every part of the pilot ready. Staff access is still being arranged, and the fallback instructions have not yet been tried by the afternoon team.

“We have two realistic choices,” I say. “A smaller, supervised pilot on Friday, if the readiness checks pass. Or a delay while we complete the wider preparation.”

“How much smaller?” Daniel asks.

“One centre, as discussed, but only two classes whose staff and learners agree to participate. We keep the existing contact process available. No automatic expansion.”

Rui looks at me. “Supervised by whom?”

“That's one of the costs.”

I turn the laptop so we can all see the empty line under support. It is uncomfortable to present a plan with blanks, but less uncomfortable than allowing somebody to mistake a blank for free labour.

We calculate the overlap between London opening hours and our working day in Shanghai. Direct support during the centre's morning would take part of our evening. Daniel can rearrange some work, but he cannot make those hours vanish. Rui already has a family commitment on Friday night. He says so without offering a detailed defence.

“I can cover the earlier period,” I say. “I can't promise the entire evening.”

Daniel writes both limits down. “We'd also need to postpone part of the reporting work. There aren't spare people waiting to do this.”

We call Elena with the two choices. She listens while Daniel explains the staffing implications. Then she asks whether two classes are enough to learn anything useful.

“Enough to observe the handover and change process,” I say. “Not enough to claim that every centre is ready.”

“And if neither class changes its time?”

“Then we learn less about real changes. We can rehearse with test data, but we should report that separately.”

She nods slowly. “Thank you for making that distinction.”

The delay has its own difficulties. Priya has already moved shifts to make training possible. A later date would mean arranging cover again. The current system causes duplicated paperwork, and another delay leaves that burden in place. Elena does not want another promise that preparation will become perfect if everyone simply waits longer.

“Could we keep adding conditions until a pilot is impossible?” she asks.

“Yes,” Rui says. “But these conditions aren't about having every feature. They're about staff being able to use the limited version safely.”

I hear the sharpness in his voice. Before Elena has to defend her question, I add, “We should distinguish essential conditions from improvements we'd like. Access and a working fallback are essential. A more convenient report can wait.”

Daniel asks me to put that distinction into the decision note. He does not choose a date on the call. Elena needs to check whether the proposed classes are suitable and whether the centre can support learners who prefer telephone contact.

Afterwards, Daniel points to the green box. “People have been planning around this for weeks.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?” He rubs his eyes. “I need something more useful than a list of reasons it might go wrong.”

The sentence lands badly. I have brought choices, costs, and conditions. For a moment I want to close the report and let him decide without me.

Instead, I say, “I think we need to discuss what you expect from my recommendation. Could we do that tomorrow, privately?”

He looks surprised, then checks his calendar. “Half past ten.”

On the train home, I reread the decision note. I remove a sentence that begins obviously. Nothing about this is obvious to everyone involved. I replace it with the evidence for the smaller option and the circumstances that would make me recommend delay.

At home, Maya asks why I am still holding my phone over my dinner.

“I have a difficult conversation tomorrow.”

“Can it happen over cold noodles?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps eat first.”

I put the phone on the counter. Maya's fifth design is face down beside the soy sauce. She has got the woman's words back onto the page, she tells me. Tomorrow somebody else will read them aloud in the client room.

“Would you like me to look again?”

“No. That's actually the trouble. Everybody gets a look. Nobody remembers whose idea it was to ask the woman in the first place.”

She twists noodles round one chopstick until they come away in a single lump. I wait. She says she would like five minutes at the review to describe the interviews herself. She can live with losing the headline. Listening to somebody else explain her research is harder.

“Five minutes in the room,” I say.

“Exactly. Can you pass the vinegar?”

My phone lights up. From across the table the screen is too small to read. I pass the vinegar. She tells me what the woman said after she put the bicycle down. It is a funny story, and halfway through it I realise Maya has had this story for weeks and I have never once asked.

phrases.en: That is one of the costs.
I can’t promise the entire evening.
phrases.zh: 说明可投入时间的上限

phrases.en: Essential conditions are different from improvements.
phrases.zh: 区分启动条件与期望优化

practice.grammar: 练习条件句中的明确后果：If the readiness checks fail, we will delay the pilot. 再用 provided that 写一个带前提的建议，避免省略关键条件。
practice.pronunciation: 对比重音：A smaller pilot / on Friday；a delay / with wider preparation。分两组各读三次，用停顿让听者听清方案与代价的对应关系。

questions.a: A smaller supervised pilot if essential checks pass, or a delay for further preparation.

questions.q: What does Maya want to do at the review?
questions.a: She wants five minutes to explain the interviews she conducted.

questions.q: What can rehearsal with test data not prove?
questions.a: It cannot prove how an actual class-time change works for real participants.

roleplay.context: 你扮演 Andy，向 Daniel 解释排期取舍，不把所有风险混成一个结论。

turns.line: We have already promised staff time for Friday.
turns.cue: 承认延期成本，然后提出两个选择

turns.line: Can you cover the whole evening?
turns.cue: 说明真实时间边界和需要另行安排的覆盖

turns.line: Why can’t the extra report wait?
turns.cue: 说明它可以等待，并指出真正必要的条件

practice.transfer: 用英语比较搬家当天的两个方案：当天只搬必需品，或推迟一天全部搬完。说出各自成本、一个决定条件，并给出有前提的建议。
practice.retell: 脱稿做九十秒决策简报，依次说明目标、两项选择、人员代价、证据局限与下一步；不要把暂定日期说成承诺。

translations.21-2: 它待在日程表的绿色方框里，看起来比周围的一切都更确定。
translations.21-3: 这是一个可能的试点日期，并不是我们在项目前期已经澄清过的演示截止日期。
translations.21-4: 可我仍感觉到那股熟悉的诱惑：用一个整齐的词，代替一份其实还没理清的约定。
translations.21-5: 哪里的周五，做什么工作，又需要满足哪些条件？
translations.21-8: Daniel把预算表放在日程表旁边。
translations.21-9: “中心已经预留了工作人员的时间。
translations.21-10: 如果改期，是要付出代价的。”
translations.21-14: 两边的代价我都需要看清楚。”
translations.21-15: 他的语气平平，并没有生气。
translations.21-17: 内部测试中重复发送通知的问题已经修正，相关检查现在都通过了。
translations.21-18: 但这不代表试点的每个环节都已准备好。
translations.21-19: 工作人员的账号权限仍在安排中，下午班也还没有试过备用流程说明。
translations.21-20: “我们有两个现实可行的选择。”我说。
translations.21-21: “如果准备情况检查通过，就在周五开展规模更小、有人监督的试点。
translations.21-22: 或者推迟，先完成更全面的准备。”
translations.21-25: “按之前讨论的，只选一个中心，而且只选两节工作人员和学员都同意参与的课。
translations.21-26: 现有的联系流程继续保留。
translations.21-31: 我把电脑转过去，让大家都能看到支持安排下面的空白一行。
translations.21-32: 拿出一份有空白的计划让人不自在，但总比让人误以为那片空白代表免费劳动力要好。
translations.21-33: 我们计算了伦敦营业时间与上海工作时间的重合部分。
translations.21-34: 在中心的上午提供直接支持，会占用我们一部分晚间时间。
translations.21-35: Daniel可以调整一些工作，但无法让这些工时凭空消失。
translations.21-36: Rui周五晚上已经有家庭安排。
translations.21-37: 他直接说了出来，没有详细解释来为自己辩护。
translations.21-40: Daniel把这两个限制都记了下来。
translations.21-41: “我们还需要推迟一部分报表工作。
translations.21-42: 没有闲着的人等着来做这些事。”
translations.21-43: 我们带着这两个选择给Elena打电话。
translations.21-44: Daniel说明人员安排上的影响时，她一直听着。
translations.21-45: 然后她问，两节课是否足以让我们获得有用的经验。
translations.21-46: “足够观察交接和修改流程。”我说。
translations.21-47: “但不足以说明每个中心都已准备好。”
translations.21-48: “如果两节课都没有修改时间呢？”
translations.21-49: “那我们对真实修改能了解的就少一些。
translations.21-50: 可以用测试数据演练，但汇报时应该单独说明。”
translations.21-54: 为了安排培训，Priya已经调整过班次。
translations.21-55: 如果改到更晚的日期，就得重新安排人员顶班。
translations.21-56: 现有系统会产生重复的文书工作，再推迟一次，这个负担就还得继续。
translations.21-57: Elena不想再听到这样的承诺：只要大家再多等一等，准备工作就能做到完美。
translations.21-58: “我们会不会一直增加条件，直到试点根本无法开展？”她问。
translations.21-60: “但这些条件不是要求功能一应俱全。
translations.21-61: 而是要让工作人员能安全地使用这个有限版本。”
translations.21-62: 我听出了他语气里的尖锐。
translations.21-63: 不等Elena为自己的问题辩解，我就补充道：“我们应该区分必要条件和希望做的改进。
translations.21-64: 能正常登录，以及可用的备用流程，都是必要条件。
translations.21-66: Daniel让我把这个区别写进决策记录。
translations.21-67: 他没有在电话里定下日期。
translations.21-68: Elena还需要确认拟定的课程是否合适，以及中心是否有能力支持更愿意接电话的学员。
translations.21-69: 之后，Daniel指着那个绿色方框。
translations.21-70: “大家围绕这个日期，已经安排了好几个星期。”
translations.21-74: “我需要比一份罗列各种出错理由的清单更有用的东西。”
translations.21-76: 我带来的明明有选择、成本和条件。
translations.21-77: 有那么一瞬间，我想合上报告，让他自己决定算了。
translations.21-78: 但我还是说：“我觉得我们需要聊聊，你希望我的建议具体提供什么。
translations.21-80: 他看起来有些意外，然后看了看日历。
translations.21-82: 坐车回家的路上，我重新读了一遍决策记录。
translations.21-83: 我删掉了一个以“显然”开头的句子。
translations.21-84: 这件事里，没有什么是所有相关人员都觉得显而易见的。
translations.21-85: 我改为写下支持缩小范围方案的证据，以及哪些情况会让我建议推迟。
translations.21-86: 到家后，Maya问我为什么吃着晚饭还举着手机。
translations.21-91: 我把手机放到厨房台面上。
translations.21-92: Maya的第五版设计反扣在酱油瓶旁边。
translations.21-93: 她告诉我，那位女士说的话总算又回到了版面上。
translations.21-94: 明天，会有另一个人在客户面前把那些话念出来。
translations.21-97: 说起来，问题就出在这儿。
translations.21-99: 可最初是谁提议去采访那位女士的，已经没人记得了。”
translations.21-100: 她拿一根筷子绕着面条，直到面条结成一团，一起被挑了起来。
translations.21-102: 她说她想在评审会上要五分钟，亲自讲讲那些访谈。
translations.21-103: 标题保不住，她可以接受。
translations.21-104: 更难受的是听别人介绍她做的调研。
translations.21-105: “你想在会上有五分钟自己讲。”我说。
translations.21-109: 隔着一张桌子，那点大的屏幕上写了什么，我看不清。
translations.21-111: 她跟我讲起那位女士放下自行车后说了什么。
translations.21-112: 那故事挺逗，听到一半我才意识到，Maya已经把它藏在心里好几个星期，而我一次都没问过。
